@C_Barraud’s Friday Brief had a lot on Thursday’s market selloff, but also a couple of posts on regional Fed presidents who seemed unmoved, even as markets have treated the tech selloff as a reason for the Fed to potentially back off.

Since the Nasdaq 100 started its 14.7% decline on October 6, through Thursday’s close, CME FedWatch odds of a hike at December’s FOMC fell from 86% to 67%. They bounced back to about 78% after Friday’s jobs beat, per Reuters.

Since October 6, daily Nasdaq 100 moves and changes in December hike pricing have a 0.61 correlation, or about 0.7 bp of hikes per 1% move.

Three Fed hawks spoke Thursday and Friday. None of them mentioned stocks as a reason to wait:

▪ Cleveland’s Hammack, who dissented for a hike last week, said Thursday in Zurich that “inflation has moved in the wrong direction” since March, with headline PCE at 3.6% and core at 3.1%. She called the pressures “relatively broad based, reflecting both supply and demand.” Her conclusion: “I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance,” preferably “through more frequent smaller adjustments.”
▪ Richmond’s Barkin (a 2027 voter) told CNBC Thursday: “Unemployment’s near record lows, and inflation is too high. That means the path is pretty straightforward. The question, of course, is pace.” He sees policy as “a little bit accommodative” and inflation as “the most important risk right now.” His only market worry was who’s carrying the risk on the more than $500 billion of hyperscaler debt.
▪ St. Louis’s Musalem called inflation “a regressive tax, a distortionary tax” on Friday, per Reuters, and told Bloomberg that today’s excess inflation is “coming both from negative supply shocks related to the Middle East and demand forces coming related to the AI build.” He added: “We need to make monetary policy for the economy of the day.”

Musalem’s AI point is a touch ironic. The market has been pricing AI weakness as a reason for fewer hikes, while the hawks see AI spending as part of the inflation problem.

The caveat, of course, is that the hawks aren’t the committee, and the core seems to be in no hurry. New York’s Williams, a permanent voter, and part of the "troika" at the top of the Fed, spoke Friday in Frankfurt. 

While he agreed that “Inflation is absolutely too high. It’s been too high for too long,” he said inflation expectations “remain well anchored” and “We’re seeing wage growth be consistent with our 2% goal.” He also backed last week’s statement that this is “an appropriate time to accumulate more information.” 

Notably though Williams didn't cite stocks according to the reports. His case for patience rests on anchored expectations and wages. The October CPI on November 10 will be the next test for the hawks and the core.

BREAKING: US imports of computers, computer accessories, and semiconductors surged +$12.1 billion in September, to a record $86.9 billion.

This marks the 2nd-largest monthly increase in history, following the record +$14.7 billion increase in July 2026.

Since the start of 2024, imports of computers, computer accessories, and semiconductors have more than quadrupled.

YoY, these imports rose +151%, the largest YoY increase on record, compared with peak annual growth of just +34% during the 2000 Dot-Com Boom.

Based on September's figures, these imports are now running at an annualized rate above $1.0 trillion for the first time.

US demand for technology hardware is exploding.

“If the *legal* system can't stop millions of foreigners from *illegally* entering the country, then the legal system is some combination of biased and impotent.”

To clarify again, the legal system does not allocate resources toward problems. In this context of holding back executive overreach, what the legal system does is rule whether executive or legislative actions are legal. Border security is an executive and legislative branch function.

“Every week there’s a story of a criminal with a long rap sheet being released and committing yet another crime.”

Sure, but at this level of conversation we focus on math rather than anecdotes, right? Crime is trending *down* over decades, despite the talking points we often hear. As a result, voters don’t typically put crime in their top slot for what they vote on even though it trends here on right-of-center social media that we're both swimming in. In areas where it’s a growing problem, I’m right there with you that it should be fixed. That’s mostly a function of putting politicians into power that will write laws that give harsher sentences to repeat offenders.

“The legal system and the agencies aren’t even trying to find the fraud.”

The Justice Department is currently run by Republicans. They could put more resources there. All the DOGE public focus on fraud amounted to little. Fraud should be prosecuted of course, but it often gets over-emphasized in political discourse because it’s the easy button. It’s politicians’ way of saying they don’t want to cut benefits or raise taxes (unpopular), and instead they claim there’s this massive room to cut down on fraud (good soundbite, everyone’s against fraud, let’s fix the budget that way). And then when they’re in power, fraud is peanuts as a percentage.

“The only reason anyone would be against voter ID is because they want to cheat.”

Then the legislative branch should have passed voter ID. Part of the issue is they overreached. They wanted super strict rules that would have made it so that even most driver’s licenses wouldn’t qualify as a voting ID. Additionally, they wanted it to apply right away to these 2026 elections, and the various federal and state document offices (Passports, Birth Certificates, etc) are not fit to handle a sharp influx of document changes that would be needed in those few months (women updating their last name on birth certificates which they never bothered to do before, now that their driver’s license isn’t even sufficient to vote, etc). I know you are not naïve, so you get the background debate there. Those in favor of voter ID also find it politically favorable to add frictions to voting (fewer younger, poorer voters), and they pushed hard here, for this election. Those against voter ID also find it politically favorable to reduce frictions to voting (more younger, poorer voters). In this latest move, voter ID proponents tried too hard to be as strict as possible and couldn’t get it done because there were actually serious issues with their proposal that get glossed over by partisans. Strategic error on their part. Pushing for a driver’s license to vote or phasing things in over years could have brought in wider support and would have a had a higher chance, compared to what they tried. And again, all of this is a legislative issue, not a judicial one.

Regarding border security and partisanship, Biden had a higher rate of annual border apprehensions than any modern president. A big issue was that there were far more people trying to cross the border, given the Covid backdrop. I think border security should have been an even bigger issue, but it’s important to understand that baseline context. And then when there was a bipartisan bill in 2024 to put more resources on the border, it was Republicans who blocked it because they wanted it to be a live issue for the 2024 elections (which, from a strict strategy perspective, probably worked out).

And no, I don’t support calls to execute Elon. I publicly pushed back against a related call to imprison him and seize the companies.
